I tried a few times in the past but I always ended up going back to Windows after a while. Maybe I didn't have strong enough reasons to migrate but I also felt overwhelmed by all the changes at the same time (yeah I did dual-boot but it didn't help much).

So I decided to try a different approach this time.

I got a second computer, put Linux on it and I'm running both machines side by side, migrating stuff a bit at a time.

I started with win software that's already opensource so it's just a matter of moving data (for example LibreOffice, GIMP, Calibre, VLC - I'm using only Linux for web surfing and docs needs now and it's feeling very good so far).

In the meantime I'm trying to find Linux alternatives to win-only applications, thanks to this sub I found out about Clementine and I'm already using it to manage my music library.

I'm still not sure about replacements for Exact Audio copy (cdparanoia?) and mp3 tag editor (no idea about this one, any help is appreciated :))

Then I'll check for remaining apps, following this sub closely is a great help.

Last step will be games, I'm planning to start with older ones so there's a greater chance they'll work with Wine/Crossover/PoL.

After all that I expect it'll be a very few things left so dual-boot won't be a problem anymore (for games I already know don't work because of DX11, example The Witcher 3).

Most important: I'm taking my time. Win7 will be still supported (even if not mainstream) for the next 5 years so there's no rush.

Maybe it's just me but I find this approach feels a lot more comfortable than anything I tried before, I just wished to share it.

I also hope you won't mind if I ask for opinions on software replacements every now and then.

p.s. I believe my reasons are strong enough now. W10 telemetry can be blocked so it doesn't worry me much but I don't tolerate forced upgrades, especially drivers that are not even "theirs".
I also don't like that I can't trust anything about windows anymore, after reading about how they don't provide details about updates and mixing "new features" with security fixes so, while still on seven, I definitely disabled windows update and I won't use it anymore (even if I hate to not install security fixes).

p.s.2 I'm using Slackware with MATE desktop, had to upgrade to current because the stable is too old for very recent notebooks, it's working very well anyway.

TL;DR I wish to share a different approach to switching to Linux: 2 computers running side by side instead of dual boot and not rushing it, it feels a lot more comfortable to me.

EDIT: I wish to thank everyone for their suggestions, I'll try them all. I'm quite confident I can "persevere" this time, I'll post back in about six months anyway, just to tell you how it went :)

I tried several distros and even if everyone says Slackware is "unfriendly" I find it's the one that gives me the least problems (yes even less than Ubuntu/derivatives) - for 2 reasons:

1 - when you install it you don't get all the software you need but you get all the libraries configured to be compatible with each other, so I know that if I need to add an application, in most cases I add that single application and I'm done. No tons of additional packages nor libraries = no conflicts that I wouldn't know how to solve.

2 - it's completely standard. It doesn't make weird changes to packages nor to configuration files so it's easier to understand than "easy" distros and I also know that I can follow original documentation from project sites and I can do my own changes without the risk of breaking something else not related to what I'm doing.

Point 2- standard. This. A million times this. So many times distros tweak install locations so user installed programs don't go in /usr/local/bin or muck up other stuff. You can read about "Linux" and just use Slackware. To me, you have to read about Ubuntu /debian/other to use Ubuntu /debian/other.

The only time I have hosed Linux systems is through using apt. It fucks up and is the elephant in the room. It is not great. Not mission critical. A lot of people can use it, but it just hands over too much for me.

Slackware just works. Mostly!!
